resenas.frase: The rock legends return with a tightly focused album that stands as a counterargument to pop-culture doomsaying
It’s not that 'Carnaval De Luz' is bad. It isn’t. It’s just humdrum

Carnaval De Luz finds U2 50 years after their formation with the same four members and the same desire to shake things up. The album provides a convincing answer to the question of why they keep doing what they do
U2 return with a defiant and celebratory record that captures them still at the height of their powers
Bono and co. return to full strength with a celebration of hope over despair

This is not a radical reinvention of Rattle And Hum-to-Achtung Baby magnitude, or even a wilful evolution akin to that from How To Dismantle An Atom Bomb to No Line On Th Horizon. The ghosts of U2's past are summoned in numbers, though they are frequently mischievously partnered to interestingly inc
Letting loose and finding renewed purpose, U2 have delivered one of their most fun and engaging albums with Carnaval De Luz, a celebratory injection of positive vibes to both the world and this band
On their first album of new songs in nearly a decade, even earnest Bono-isms carry weight amid music that is impassioned and rejuvenated
Irish rock’s crazy diamonds shine on brighter than ever
They sound ambitious and engaged in their 50th year, swinging for the fences and hitting more targets than not. There’s still some gas in the tank
On their 16th studio album, U2 revisit their familiar sound while exploring themes of faith, hope and humanity

Ambitious but accessible, catchy but substantial, they've returned with a record that feels energized and alive, as though they have once again arrived at the start of something inventive and exciting

At times thrilling, ‘Carnaval De Luz’ isn’t perfect, but it nonetheless contains some of U2’s best and most effective music for a decade. Shrugging off the cynics, it’s the work of a band with an appetite for the future

With Carnaval De Luz they are not reinventing themselves or trying to be the current flavour of the month. What they do with this album is revisit their older glories and create new music and sounds. And as a legacy band it is near impossible to not compare their new music to their classic albums
The Irish legends' best work in 25 years homages their eras, brings Brian Eno to bear on keys and even wheels out the late Dolly Parton
With a sense of appreciation for their own longevity, U2 return with their first new album in nearly a decade to ask: What if rock’n’roll is the friends we made along the way?
Despite Bono’s protests, a rock and roll band can’t save the world, but they may just be able to save themselve
On their sixteenth studio album, the Irish legends sound more playful than preachy for the first time in a long time
Their communion, while undeniably luminous in intent, doesn’t always translate as it should
The Irish stadium legends’ latest is pedantic and ambiguous, rife with centrist pandering that ends up saying nothing at all

resenas.frase: A masterpiece from the greatest band of their generation

When a band reaches a certain size, a lot of people start claiming they were better before they got big. We defy anyone to listen to 'Dopamine Chamber' and make that claim in good faith - this is a band firing on all cylinders and staking their claim to be the best band of their generation
After the surreal technicolour dreams of 'Romance', Fontaines D.C. have landed back on Earth to dissect our fractured reality. The result is something truly special
As Dublin’s finest reach stadium level, album five dives deeper into the extremes of ‘Romance’ for a dark but exhilarating reflection of end times
This is a beguiling, endlessly inventive and frequently astonishing fifth LP from a group at increasing ease with being the best band of their generation
Incredibly, the intensity and complexity of Grian Chatten’s voice has deepened since the much-lauded 'Romance'
Fifth album finds Dublin quintet sounding grandiose and exhilarating, evolving while refusing to compromise any of their identity
A mirror to our times casting back a stark, frightening image
Dark, daring and decidedly enthralling, Fontaines D.C.'s fifth album Dopamine Chamber is the sound of a band completely in a league of their own

If Romance was the first time Fontaines D.C. raised their head over the parapet, Dopamine Chamber is the storming of the Winter Palace. It is the absolute victory we always dream of, when the outsiders take over
Dopamine Chamber sounds like a busted limbic system that forces you to let all of the emotions hit you at once
A wrecking ball of innovation that proves the band are a power unto themselves, and each new challenge posed by the release of a new album continues to draw out their undeniable genius
The band incorporates a great many influences, but they make everything their own distinct sound. It is an album of discovery and gets better with each spin on the turntable
Dopamine Chamber finds Fontaines moving even further away from the live guitar emphasis of their earlier work – embracing new styles in ways that are, by turns, liberating and devastating
If you've already started building your AOTY list but haven't listened to Dopamine Chamber yet, make sure you leave a slot open
The Irish band's fifth album is a synth-heavy reinvention, jagged and unnerving at multiple turns
On Dopamine Chamber, the Irish band reaches further into electronic moodiness while delivering hard-hitting reflections on how to stay sane — and maybe even hopeful — these days

Dopamine Chamber is no different; while not too far removed from the sonic sensibilities of Romance, the darker tone and existential themes keep the band's meditations on the modern world as potent as ever
As dark chroniclers of their age, Fontaines D.C. are here to illuminate the gloom

‘Dopamine Chamber’ is Fontaines D.C. rambling about the worst bits of the modern world – environmental collapse, extreme wealth, political violence – over some of the prettiest instrumentals the band have written
Dopamine Chamber is larger than life in a way that very few bands can achieve, and although it dives into feelings of digital isolation, it manages to feel like a collective experience
Dopamine Chamber is the sound of Fontaines DC becoming megastars. Is bigger always better?
Fontaines D.C. push deeper into synthetic territory on Dopamine Chamber, balancing stadium-sized melodies with restless experimentation and darker texture
As they fine-tune their stylistic evolution, the perfect balance is yet to be discovered
Balances profound cynicism and genuine beauty as its ice-hearted stadium rock grows to darkly apocalyptic proportions

Even with just one spin, it becomes evident that the album seems more like three distinct EPs, and one single, that have been collected. This might seem a weird way of assessing music, but the album clearly shifts gears after every three songs
Grian Chatten and co swap guitars for icy synths and confront a world of endless conflict, digital dependency and creeping despair
While there is no doubt Fontaines D.C. will rightly go down as one of the era’s greats, this LP shows them struggling to close the gap between ambition and lasting impact
I don't know if Dopamine Chamber is destined for next-level success and massive airplay, but if there's a rock band built for the modern era and its sensibilities, it's Fontaines D.C
The fifth album from Dublin’s Fontaines D.C. trades post-punk for polished pop-rock jams

While Romance wasn’t the most cohesive LP, the majority of its tracks included beguiling hooks and textbook popcraft. Dopamine, too, is more a grab bag of songs than a precisely outlined set. Unfortunately, in Dopamine’s case, the pop savvy appears less consistently, leaving various tunes groping fo
Both in terms of indie rock writ large and the band’s own artistic development, the Dubliners’ latest isn’t nearly as revolutionary as 2024’s Romance
Dopamine Chamber in three words, then. Should do better
Doubles down on synthesizers and chokes out their previous sound; most of the album ends up sounding the same
The album’s best songs lean into sinister undertones with relish

The Mancunian icon confronts modern malaise, fractured times and the shifting sands of the now with restless, life-affirming rock ’n’ roll with an added post punk inventiveness

The Age of Everything isn’t the first of Johnny Marr’s solo albums to be able to stand on its own merits, but it’s the one that does it most confidently, a polished, consistent record on which he becomes a singer and guitarist rather than a singing guitarist

Four decades on, he remains a class act, still curious, still innovative and still relentlessly cool. If ‘The Age Of Everything’ is about embracing possibility, Johnny Marr embodies the very best of everything music has to offer

The Age Of Everything is an exemplar of all those elements that have made Marr's solo career such a satisfying success: big, hooky songs, hummable melodies, insightful lyrics and a distinctive guitar sound

Marr isn’t releasing The Age of Everything as a grand statement of career intent; he has afforded himself the right to comfortably write tunes within his wheelhouse and release them to a dedicated audience

Iommi’s vision and intentions make for a seriously powerful set of tunes that will keep plenty of Metalheads more than happy
From The Dark is the sort of album where nothing is out of place - everything adds to its integrity, and to the brooding atmosphere of foreboding. Print edition only
The whole thing is biblically, sometimes exhaustingly epic, but a timely reminder of Iommi's pioneering musicianship. Print edition only
A reaffirmation of the man’s elemental power and enduring importance
From The Dark is a strong, latter career highlight that sees Iommi seamlessly pickup from where he left off over a decade ago in what hopefully ignites the start of a new era for Iommi
Teaming with Norwegian vocalist Jørn Lande, the 78-year-old Black Sabbath guitarist gets back to heavy-metal basics on a proudly uncompromising new solo album

From the Dark is probably the best album Black Sabbath guitarist Tony Iommi has released under his own name. It’s definitely good, but it’s also so typical of his music over the past four decades that it’s hard to get very excited about

Considering that Tony Iommi is one of, if not the, most significant heavy metal figure in the current landscape, you’d be hard-pressed to find anyone who doesn’t believe From The Dark to be a deeply significant moment in his career
Doomheads may regret this new record isn't an experimental black mass of riffs. Fans of lacy-sleeved hard rock, however, will lean into the tuneful thunderstorm. Print edition only
